title: How does the UK contribute to the EU budget?

breadcrumb.text: How does the UK contribute to the EU budget?

body.text: Each year the UK government makes a contribution to the EU budget. This is mainly based on the size of the UK’s economy relative to the economies of the other EU Member States.

body.h2: Where does the money for the budget come from?
Where does the money for the budget come from?
body.text: Member states give 75% of customs, agriculture, sugar and isoglucose levies to the EU. The remaining 25% are then kept to cover the costs of administration.

body.h2: Where does the money for the budget come from?
Where does the money for the budget come from?
body.text: Member States contribute a standardised 0.3% of their total VAT income. However, there are exceptions to the rate for Austria (0.225%), Germany (0.15%), Sweden and the Netherlands (both 0.10%).

body.h2: Where does the money for the budget come from?
Where does the money for the budget come from?
body.text: Member States also a standard percentage of their Gross National Income (GNI). It basically counts all income earned by UK residents regardless of where it was earned. Member States’ GNI-based contributions cover the remainder of the EU budget, up to a cap of 1.24%.

body.h2: Why are EU budget contributions sometimes revised?
body.text: Eurostat carries out annual audits and can place EU-wide or country-specific revisions on measurements they’d like to see improved. Member states are then given a timeframe to make these changes, which then determines whether they’ve under or over paid.
